en: In well-established temples, hermitages, monasteries, palaces, dwellings, and pavilions,
the lowering of the banner should be performed, having carefully examined the middle, the base, and the tip of the excellent door.
Having carefully observed the foremost [parts] from the center of the excellent gateway,

one should firmly plant the victory banners at the pinnacle of the middle of that sublime gate, after having looked evenly upon the divine abodes, the incense halls, the monasteries, the palatial mansions, the chambers, and the assembly halls.
[They may be made of gold, rubies, stone, silver, fine clay, or wood;
well-proportioned, straight, firm, brilliant, equal in three parts, and well-jointed.]

Whether made of gold, jewels, crystal, silver, or even of clay, wood, or the finest materials, it should be well-situated, straight, firm, brilliantly radiant, and properly arranged with its three parts in equal proportions.
In the pavilions of the Jineśvarakūṭa temple, the height is the standard measure and the width of the door is twice as long;
in the shrines that are half that measure, the same applies to the crosswise measurement, even with the excellent enclosures.

The dimensions of the multi-storied palaces, the chambers, and the assembly halls of the Lord of Victors are such that the doors are twice their length; the turrets and the great halls are half that measure. They are well-proportioned, and for the Victor as well, it is exactly so.
The banners, resembling water-pots, filled with the nectar of the wisdom of the Lord of Munis,
and having the form of the orb of the moon, are pouring forth [nectar] upon the body of the monastery.

As many victory banners as there are, they are like vases; filled with the nectar of the wisdom of the Lord of Sages, they are by nature the mandala of sublime Nectar-Light. Having been thoroughly cleansed, they constitute the body of the temple.

Having visualized that which has arisen from it as the form of a *caitya* born from the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, its body adorned with parasols and garments, one should bind it with flowers, cloth, and five threads; then, having placed it [upon the base], one should recite the mantra while holding a vajra in hand.

To summon it: having visualized the form of a stūpa arisen from *bhrūṃ*, adorned with parasols, garments, and ornaments, bound with flowers, garments, and five threads, one should perform the recitation while maintaining equanimity together with the vajra.
Standing in front with the mantra of the Lord of Jinas, he stands on the right with the mantra of the Crest of the Banner;
standing in the west with the mantras of Amitābha, he [performs] the ornamentation of the Sage in the north with the mantra.

Those dwelling in the east [recite] the secret mantra of the Lord of Victors; those dwelling in the south, the secret mantra of the Pinnacle of Victory; those dwelling in the west, the secret mantra of Amitābha; and from the north as well, with the mind of the Ornament of the Sage.
Having proceeded in a clockwise direction all around, holding flowers, garments, and thread in his hands,
he should perform the vase-consecration with effort, having first established it with flowers, water-offerings, ritual arts, and so forth.

Moving in a clockwise direction, one should circumambulate completely; with hands holding flowers, garments, and threads, one should diligently perform the consecration with vases containing flowers, water for offerings, fruits, and so forth.
Accompanied by the clamor of drums, lutes, conchs, kāhala-trumpets, and bells,
together with the auspicious songs of the women of Īriṇī.
Together with the teacher, he performed the communal recitation.
With the sounds of musical instruments,
incense, and copper horns, accompanied by the resonance of water-pitchers, the Vajrācāryas, together with the auspicious melodic songs of the women, [performed].

The mantra of the Victor Vairocana: Oṃ sūkṣme 2 samaye 2 śānte 2 dānte 2 asamārope nirālambe nirākule nirvāṇe yaśovati mahāteje sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhānādhiṣṭhite svāhā. [Recite this] twenty-one times in the east.

The mantra of the Victorious One Vairocana is: Oṃ sukṣme sukṣme same samaye śānte śānte dānte dānte āsamarope nīrālaṃbhe nīrākule nirvāṇe yaśovati mahāteje sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhānādhiṣṭhite svāhā. Recite this twenty-one times from the east.

The Great Mantra of Dhvajāgrakeyūrī: Oṃ Dhvajāgrakeyūre! Victory! Victory! Be victorious! Be victorious! O Jayavāhinī! O Śaṅkarī! O Prabhākari! O Prabhaṅkari! O Prabhañjani! Destroy! Destroy! Delude! Delude! O Blessed One! O Jayavāhinī! O Jayottarī! Grind! Grind! Crush! Crush! Laugh! Laugh! Devour! Devour! Hūṃ! Hūṃ! He! He! Laghu! Laghu! O Lambodarī! O Three-eyed One! O Four-faced One! O Four-tusked One! O Four-armed One! O Wielder of sword, mace, discus, trident, vajra, and armor! Protect me, O Blessed One!

*Krūṇamati jambudhvaje buddhāvalokite | rakṣa rakṣa saṃ sarvatathāgatāvalokite svāhā | guṇarājiprabhāsottame svāhā | candrārkapramiṇe svāhā | sarvagrahanakṣatradharmikaraṇi svāhā | rakṣa rakṣemaṃ sthānaṃ sarvabhayebhyaḥ svāhā |* Once from the south (dakṣiṇena).
The King of Mantras of Amitābha:
Oṃ amite amite amitodbhave amitasaṃbhave amitavikrānte amitavikrāntagāmini amitavikrāntagāmini amitāyurdade dharmadhātujñānagaganaparikīrtite sarvakarmakleśakṣayaṃkariye svāhā.
oṃ āmita āmita āmitodbhave | āmitasaṃbhave āmitavikrāntagate āmitāyurdade dharmadhātujñānagaṇaparikīrtite sarvakarmakleśakṣayaṃkari svāhā | Recite this seven times from the west.
The mantra of the *Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra-dhāraṇī*:
the mantra of the dhāraṇī of the Vajragarbha-ornamentation.

Oṃ bodhi 2! O you who range within the domain of all Bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas! Dharā 2! Harā 2! Praharā 2! O bearer of the great mind of awakening (mahābodhicitta)! Culu 2! O you who are impelled by rays of light, consecrated by all Tathāgatas, sky of qualities, radiance of pure qualities! Mili 2! O you who are established in the expanse of the sky! Śama 2! Praśama 2! O pacifier of all sins, purifier of all sins! Hulu 2! O you who have set out upon the path of great awakening, ocean of all Tathāgatas! Svāhā!

*Praśama praśama | sarvapāpapraśamana sarvapāpaviśodhani hulu hulu | mahābodhimārgasaṃprasthite | sarvatathāgatamudre svāhā | Seven times with the north.* (Seven times from the north.)

Oṃ, O you who are radiant with a hundred jewels of all the Tathāgatas, blaze, blaze! O you whose womb is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), svāhā! Those phenomena which arise from a cause, their cause the Tathāgata has explained, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
oṃ sarvatathāgatamaṇiśaptadīpte jvala jvala dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā | ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hyavadat | teṣāṃ ca yo nirodha evaṃvādī mahāśramaṇaḥ | From the east itself—
*pūrveṇaiva*.
Thus ends the raising of the banner.
Thus it is called "bearing the victory banner."
Established upon the firm staff of Vajrāvaśūti, it is bound by thirty-two ribs;
it is a pure lotus-canopy born from the syllable *Haṃ*, shining brilliantly and radiantly on all sides.

The vajra-ābhuṭi stands firmly upon its stalk; it certainly binds the thirty-two petals. Born from the syllable *haṃ*, it is a lotus, a perfectly pure parasol, beautiful on all sides and endowed with blazing edges.

One disciplined in yoga should consecrate the parasol, which possesses a beautiful form marked with the glorious *dharmadhātu*, which is resplendent with strings of jeweled half-necklaces, and which bears the mark of victory that removes the remorse of the mind.

The form adorned and beautified by the glorious Dharma-sphere, Resplendent with the arising of garlands of half-jeweled nets, Marked by the victory that captivates the heights of the mind— Know this as the application [of the term] "Abiding on the Parasol."
Oṃ namaḥ samantabuddhabodhisattvānām āḥ candracchattrāvali svāhā. One should recite this one hundred and eight times.
One should recite one hundred and eight times;
thus [is the rite for] the parasol. Oṃ.
Thus is the [mantra] of the parasol.
The form of the beautiful vajra-staff, brilliant with the great light of the mirror of gnosis,
is established upon the Meru-lotus throne as the great banner of the lion and other [beasts], the Great Bliss.
The great mirror of primordial wisdom blazes intensely; it rests upon a beautiful vajra handle. Upon Mount Meru, a lotus seat, and a lion throne, the great victory banner of supreme joy stands.
[The mandala] fashioned from the seed-syllables A, Ka, Ga, Ma, Si, Bī, and Ja; [it contains] the Aparājita-vase, Garuḍa, Makara, and so forth;
[it is] rich in food.
Marked with a fish, a peacock, a jewel, a deer, and a lion, its form resembles the moon, a drop, a lotus, and a [sacred] seat.

Arisen from the seed-syllables *ā*, *ga*, *ma*, *ga*, *sa*, *ya*, and *i*, it is the invincible vase marked with garuḍas, makaras, fish, peacocks, deer, jewels, and lions; it possesses the form of a lotus and the lunar drop (*candrabindu*).
Oṃ āḥ, O you who possess the vajra-banner, O Victorious One, svāhā!
oṃ āḥ vajradhvajapatāke svāhā | thus [is] the banner.
Thus it is said; this belongs to Dhvaja.
The banner of the power of wisdom, of true renown, and of the supreme glory of virtues— variegated like the sprouting of the seed-syllable *yaṃ*— is raised high.
Possessing the excellence of supreme renown and qualities born of wisdom, these various kinds of food arise from the seed-syllable *paṃ*.
Oṃ āḥ vajraketu vajrapatāke adhiṣṭhāya yaṃ svāhā.
oṃ āḥ vajrake tu vajrapatāke ādhitiṣṭha phaṭ svāhā | Thus [is the mantra for] the banner.
"Ba dan" means "of the banner."
And a fly-whisk of great excellence, auspicious and full of splendor, with a variegated handle shining with excellent gems and pearls.
There were also beautiful, auspicious fly-whisks with handles fashioned from various kinds of sublime gold, precious gems, and radiant pearls.
The seed-syllable of Cāmarī is *caṃ*. Oṃ curu cāmari svāhā.
From the seed-syllable *caṃ*, there arise whisks; *oṃ tsuruścāmarisvāhā*.
Thus [are] the whisks.
Regarding the term "rnga yab," it refers to the *cāmara* (yak-tail whisk).
Through the performance of rites such as bali-offerings and homa,
he [attained] nourishment from the entire host of deities,
including those presiding over the city and its surroundings.
And one who desires merit should satisfy those born of the forest.

Through rituals such as the offering of *bali* and burnt offerings (*homa*), one should please the entire assembly of deities with a mind of expansion (*puṣṭi*), using wealth produced from cities, dwellings, and so forth, for the sake of merit.
The ritual procedure for the lowering of the banner and other [festivals], and for consecration.
This is the ritual for the consecration of images, such as victory banners and so forth.
